container.note: No minimum size was given. Use loam-based compost; move young plants up 5–7.5 cm at a time and larger ones 10–15 cm, every 2–3 years.

careNotes.text: Harvest comes 12–15 months after planting.
Remove side suckers until the bunch appears, then keep one or two.
Heavy bunches can topple the plant: support it under the bunch.
Needs good drainage; give new tissue-culture plants partial shade for about two weeks.

petSafety.note: Banana (Musa acuminata) is listed as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: Medium class: 4–6 gallons (15–23 L), 8–12 in (20–30 cm) deep. RHS: compact varieties, one per 30 cm pot.

daysToHarvest.note: Days to maturity from ICAR's terrace table.

spacing.note: Raised beds: 9–12 in (22.9–30.5 cm) (NC State); RHS gives 30 cm for compact and up to 45 cm for larger varieties.

careNotes.text: Earth up the plant about a month after transplanting.
Cover young plants with insect-proof mesh to keep caterpillars off.
Harvest as soon as heads reach a usable size and feel hard.

container.note: At least 2 gallons (7.6 L), one plant per container. No depth was given.

spacing.note: Raised beds: 6–12 in (15.2–30.5 cm) (NC State); RHS gives 30–45 cm.

careNotes.text: Sow on time: broccoli cannot stand high heat, which brings bolting and tiny heads.
Cut heads while the buds are still tight; they open fast in warm weather.
After the main head is cut, side shoots give smaller heads in about 10–12 days.

container.note: RHS: a pot or grow bag at least 30 cm wide and deep, one seed potato per 30 cm of width. NC State suggests about 30 gallons (114 L) and 2 ft deep for a full crop.

spacing.note: Raised beds: 10–12 in (25.4–30.5 cm) (NC State); RHS gives 30 cm for earlies and 37.5 cm for maincrops.

careNotes.text: In a grow bag, start half full and keep adding compost as the stems grow, up to just below the rim.
Earth up about 25–30 days after planting, and keep tubers covered: tubers turn green in light, and green tubers and leaves must not be eaten.
Containers need regular watering all season; leaves can stop rain reaching the compost, so check it.

container.note: A container at least 45 cm wide and deep, sets 10–15 cm apart.

spacing.note: Raised beds: 2–4 in (5.1–10.2 cm) (NC State); RHS gives 10–15 cm for larger bulbs.

careNotes.text: Onion does not tolerate waterlogging; use a free-draining mix.
Stop watering about two weeks before harvest. Lift when the tops dry and fall over, then cure the bulbs in shade.

petSafety.note: Onion is listed as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: One plant per grow bag, or one in a container at least 45 cm (18 in) wide. Choose compact varieties. Full-sized pumpkins don't suit containers. Only very compact bush varieties do: one per pot at least 45 cm wide, or per grow bag.

daysToHarvest.note: Well-matured fruits are harvested 85–90 days after sowing (TNAU).

spacing.note: Raised beds: 24–36 in (61–91.4 cm) (NC State); RHS gives 90 cm for bush and 1.5 m for trailing varieties.

careNotes.text: Keep fruits off damp ground. Smaller types can climb strong supports, with nets to hold the fruits.
Pick mature fruit when the skin turns pale brown; immature fruit can be picked too.
Collect and destroy fruits damaged by fruit fly.

container.note: UF/IFAS gives 2–5 gallons (7.6–19 L) for luffas in general.

spacing.note: Plants 75–90 cm apart (PAU); UF/IFAS spaces luffa 3 ft (91.4 cm) apart.

careNotes.text: Train the vine over a pandal, stakes or trellis.
Pick every 3–4 days, only tender medium-sized fruits; older ones turn fibrous.

container.note: No container size was found in the sources.

daysToHarvest.note: Annual moringa (PKM 1, PKM 2): harvest starts in the fourth month after transplanting.

careNotes.text: Pinch the tip when the seedling is about 75 cm tall to make it branch.
After harvest, cut the plant back to 90 cm; it crops again in about 4–5 months.
Regular pruning gives a bushier plant and more leaves; unpruned plants give more pods.

container.note: One plant in a pot at least 30 cm (1 ft) wide, or one per grow bag. No depth was given. RHS: a container at least 30 cm wide, one plant per pot or grow bag.

spacing.note: At least 30 cm (1 ft) apart, as the stems spread (RHS).

careNotes.text: Lift and turn the vines now and then so they don't root at the nodes, which gives small, thin tubers.
Containers dry out fast: check the compost often (daily in hot weather); tubers won't swell if the plant goes short of water.
Use pest-free planting material and clear old plant debris against sweet potato weevil.

petSafety.note: Sweet potato vine (Ipomoea batatas) is listed as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: Ginger grow-bag figure (at least 12 in, 30.5 cm, deep and wide) used for turmeric, another rhizome crop. No size was given. The rhizomes can grow thick enough to split a pot, so use a wide, sturdy one; it needs plenty of water.

daysToHarvest.note: Early varieties 7–8 months, long-duration ones about 9 months (Kerala). Punjab varieties mature in 215–240 days.

spacing.note: 15 cm between plants and 45 cm between rows (TNAU, PAU).

careNotes.text: Plant pieces of the mother or finger rhizomes.
Mulch after planting and keep the soil moist until the rhizomes sprout.
It is ready to lift when the whole plant has turned yellow and dried.
Tolerates low to medium shade, so it suits a partly shaded corner.
Cut rhizomes stain hands and clothes yellow, and the dye can cause an allergic skin reaction in some people.

evidence.text: NCCIH: we don't know enough to say whether turmeric or curcumin helps with any health purpose.
WHO lists skin diseases only as a traditional use, not as a use supported by clinical data.
The EU herbal committee accepts turmeric only for mild digestive problems, taken by mouth; it lists no skin use.

cautions.text: Curcumin on the skin can cause hives or itching.
Allergic dermatitis has been reported, most often in people who handle it regularly.
Turmeric supplements may be unsafe in pregnancy.

container.note: It can grow in a container if pruned to keep its size down; no size was given. Potted trees cope with drought less well than trees in the ground.

careNotes.text: Sow seeds from fresh fruit straight away, with the pulp removed: they stay viable for only about 2 months.
A tropical tree: it does not tolerate temperatures below about 4 °C (40 °F).
Mulch young plants.
It can spread by self-seeding.

evidence.text: WHO: neem leaf has been applied to the skin for ringworm, but controlled clinical trials are lacking. Use for skin disorders, septic wounds and boils is traditional.

cautions.text: Never swallow neem leaf: poisoning, including a cardiac arrest, has been reported.
WHO says neem leaf should not be given in pregnancy or while breastfeeding, or to children under 12.

container.note: Small flowering annuals: at least 1–3 US gal (3.8–11.4 L) of mix, 4–6 in (10.2–15.2 cm) deep. A good choice for containers; no size was given.

careNotes.text: A winter flower in Punjab: seedlings set out in October–November bloom from December to April, most in March.
Deadhead regularly to keep it flowering, and pinch out the shoot tips for a bushier plant.
Very wet or over-rich soil gives poor growth, and it won't flower in deep shade.
Watch for powdery mildew, aphids and whiteflies, and for slugs and snails on young plants.
Pot marigold is a different plant from the common marigold (genda, Tagetes).

petSafety.note: Pot marigold (Calendula officinalis) is listed as non-toxic to dogs and cats.

evidence.text: The EU herbal committee accepts calendula flower preparations, on the basis of long traditional use, for minor skin inflammation (such as sunburn) and to help minor wounds heal; only for people over 6.
The clinical studies it reviewed were too flawed for firm conclusions, and WHO lists no use supported by clinical data.

cautions.text: Skin sensitisation has been reported. Don't use it if you are allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae).

container.note: Small herbs: at least 1–3 US gal (3.8–11.4 L) of mix, 4–6 in (10.2–15.2 cm) deep. Suits a container; no size was given.

daysToHarvest.note: First harvest 150–200 days after planting; ICAR-DMAPR trials took the first cut at 5 months.

careNotes.text: Grows very well in shade; about 50% shade gave the best yields in Tamil Nadu.
Likes moist soil, but roots rot in soil that drains poorly.
Spreads by runners that root where they touch the soil, and can turn weedy.
From October planting, pick the outer leaves every two weeks from January.
Sometimes also called brahmi, a name more often used for a different plant, Bacopa monnieri.

evidence.text: The EU herbal committee accepts it, on the basis of long traditional use, as a dressing or powder to help minor wounds heal (adults).
WHO lists treating wounds, burns and ulcerous skin conditions, and preventing keloid scars, as uses supported by clinical data.

cautions.text: Don't use it if you are allergic to the carrot family (Apiaceae).
Not established for under-18s, and not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

container.note: Large containers 30–40 cm across (RHS); at least 4–6 US gal (15.1–22.7 L) of mix, 8–12 in (20.3–30.5 cm) deep (UMD). A large container 30–40 cm across, with large drainage holes.

careNotes.text: Needs lots of sun and fast-draining soil; it won't last long in shady, damp soil.
Pots dry out quickly in summer, so check them often.
Trim every year just after flowering to keep it compact; don't cut into old, bare wood.
Seed from named varieties won't come true; take cuttings instead.

petSafety.note: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses (linalool, linalyl acetate). Signs include nausea and vomiting.

evidence.text: NCCIH: lavender is promoted for use on the skin, but more high-quality research is needed for reliable conclusions about any of its uses.
WHO lists external use on burns and wounds only as a traditional use.

cautions.text: Lavender products on the skin may cause allergic reactions in some people.
A few cases of breast swelling were reported in children using lavender skin products; it isn't clear lavender caused them.

container.note: Suitable for containers; no size was given.

daysToHarvest.note: Roots harvested 18 months after planting for the most oil (TNAU, KAU).

careNotes.text: Grown from slips (divisions). Cut the tops back before planting so they lose less water.
Grows in most soils; a rich, well-drained sandy loam is best.
Tolerates salt and drought.
For the fragrant roots, the whole plant is dug up about 18 months after planting, in the dry season.
In dry areas termites may attack the roots.

container.note: Figures for Swiss chard, the same species (Beta vulgaris): at least 1.9 L of mix, 20.3 cm deep (NC State).

spacing.note: 10 cm in rows 20 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Cut the leaves again every 20 to 25 days after the first harvest. In summer, take only one harvest.
A sowing can give several cuttings: the All Green variety gives about 6 to 7 cuttings, 15 to 18 days apart.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

spacing.note: 60 cm in rows 100 cm apart (KAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Grow it up a trellis, fence or stakes; it is a vigorous climber.
Nick or scratch the seed coat before sowing to speed up germination; it needs warm temperatures to sprout.

container.note: At least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep (UMD).

spacing.note: 10.2–15.2 cm (NC State).

careNotes.text: Pick while young and tender: cut the large outer leaves and leave the inner ones to keep growing.
Give some shade as the weather turns hot; heat and dry soil make the leaves strong and bitter.

container.note: 30 cm deep, 30 cm across (RHS).

spacing.note: 10.2 cm (NC State); 15 cm in rows 30 cm apart (RHS).

careNotes.text: Harvest the swollen stems while young; left too long they turn tough, spongy and stringy.
In hot, dry spells it can turn woody or bolt, so cooler-season sowings tend to do better.

container.note: 40 cm across, 2 plants per container (Texas A&M, RHS).

spacing.note: 7.6–10.2 cm (NC State); 15–23 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: Pull roots at 3 inches (about 7.5 cm) across or smaller; bigger roots turn pungent, pithy and stringy.
Water and feed steadily; dry soil, low fertility or late harvest make the roots woody.

daysToHarvest.note: From sowing, for KAU's short-fruited variety Baby; longer-fruited varieties may take longer (KAU).

spacing.note: 75 cm in rows 75 cm apart (Telangana Horticulture, field crop).

careNotes.text: Remove side shoots until the main vine reaches the top of the trellis; for straight fruits, tie a small stone to the flower end with a long string.
Pick every 2 to 3 days with scissors or a knife while fruits are light green with soft white seeds; left too long they turn spongy and sour.

container.note: Figures for winter squash, the nearest named large-fruited cucurbit vine: at least 30.3 L of mix (37.9 L recommended), 30.5 cm deep, 1 plant per container (UMD).

spacing.note: 75–90 cm in rows 300 cm apart (PAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Fruits are mature when the stalk joining them to the vine starts to shrivel; cut with secateurs, leaving 3-4 inches (8-10 cm) of stalk.

spacing.note: 200 cm in rows 200 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Grow from cuttings of a fruiting (female) vine; plants raised from seed are often male and bear no fruit.
Give it a pandal or trellis, pinch the vine back at 5-6 nodes to make it branch, and pick fruits young, as soon as the dried flower falls off.

container.note: Figures for beans in general: at least 7.6 L of mix, 20.3 cm deep (NC State).

spacing.note: 15 cm in rows 60 cm apart (KAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Pole types need support: give stakes up to a 2 m pandal or trellis and train the vines onto it.
Water steadily but not too heavily; heavy watering gives lots of leaves at the expense of pods. Watering at flowering helps pod set.

spacing.note: 50 cm in rows 100 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: The seed coat is very hard: soak seeds for 12 to 48 hours (and scratch the coat) before sowing for faster, even germination.
It is not drought tolerant; water in dry weather. It needs little or no fertiliser.

spacing.note: 30.5 cm (NC State); 34–45 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: Corn is wind-pollinated: plant in a block or circle of at least 12 plants, not one long row, or ears fill poorly.
Pick at the milky stage, about 17 to 24 days after the first silks show: husks still green, silks brown and dry, and a pierced kernel gives milky juice.

spacing.note: 15 cm in rows 67.5 cm apart (PAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Mulch the soil soon after planting to keep moisture in and weeds down.
Harvest when most leaves turn yellow; stop watering 3-4 weeks before you dig the corms.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: 30 cm deep, 30 cm across (RHS).

spacing.note: 20 cm in rows 30 cm apart (RHS).

careNotes.text: Water during dry spells. In hot, dry weather dill bolts (flowers early) and stops producing leaves, and pots dry out very quickly.
When picking leaves, take only a few at a time and always leave at least one-third of the plant to keep growing.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: At least 15.1 L of mix (22.7 L recommended), 20.3 cm deep, 30 cm across (UMD, RHS).

spacing.note: 30 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: Fennel grows tall, so use a heavy, stable pot in a sheltered spot where it won't blow over.
If you want leaves rather than seed, cut off the flower stems as they appear so the plant keeps making new leafy growth.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

careNotes.text: Use well-drained soil. It needs only occasional watering and very little other care.
Check for spider mites and mealybugs, which can damage this plant.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: At least 15.1 L of mix (22.7 L recommended), 20.3 cm deep, 25 cm across (UMD, RHS).

careNotes.text: Parsley seed is slow to come up, often a month or more, so keep the soil moist and be patient.
In hot, sunny spells, move pots into shade to cut down on watering.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: At least 15.1 L of mix (22.7 L recommended), 20.3 cm deep, 30 cm across (UMD, RHS).

spacing.note: 45 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: In pots, water during dry spells because the compost dries quickly in hot sun, but never let it become waterlogged. Use a pot with plenty of drainage holes.
Trim lightly every year after flowering to keep it compact, but don't cut back into old wood.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: At least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep, 15 cm across (UMD, RHS).

careNotes.text: Thyme rarely needs watering except in pots during hot, dry weather. Too much water rots the roots, so use free-draining, gritty compost.
Trim lightly after flowering to keep plants compact and bushy.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: 15 cm deep, 15 cm across, 1 plant per container (RHS).

careNotes.text: Water potted oregano in dry spells, because the compost dries out quickly in hot sun, but never let it become waterlogged.
Golden or variegated oregano does better with some shade during the hottest part of the day.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: Figures for small herbs and flowering plants: at least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep (UMD).

spacing.note: 45 cm in rows 45 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Pinch off flower buds as soon as they appear. The leaves are sweetest before the plant flowers.
When harvesting, cut the stems about 15 cm (6 inches) above the soil so the plant can regrow.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

spacing.note: 20 cm in rows 100 cm apart (KAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Shade newly planted cuttings until they establish.
Give the vine a support and tie it loosely every 15–20 cm as it climbs.

spacing.note: 10 cm in rows 10 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: To harvest, cut the stems about 4–5 cm above the base and leave the rest to regrow.
Brahmi suits a hanging basket or trailing over the edge of a pot, and can even grow in shallow water.

container.note: Figures for small flowering annuals (dwarf zinnias; tall ones need more): at least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep (UMD).

careNotes.text: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves; wet foliage encourages leaf-spot and fungal disease.
Remove faded flowers to keep new blooms coming.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

careNotes.text: Don't fertilise cosmos; feeding can stop it from flowering.
Stems are thin and weak; stake or support taller plants, especially in windy spots.
Shelter tall varieties from strong wind; they may need staking.
Choose dwarf varieties for containers.

container.note: Figures for small flowering annuals: at least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep (UMD).

careNotes.text: Pinch off the top 2–3 cm of new plants at planting so they branch well.
If plants get leggy or stop flowering, cut the shoots back by about half, then feed and water to push new growth.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: Figures for small flowering annuals: at least 3.8 L of mix (11.4 L recommended), 10.2 cm deep (UMD).

careNotes.text: Pinch back the stems of young plants when they are about 10 cm tall for bushier growth.
In hot summers give balsam a mostly shaded spot.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

spacing.note: 30 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: Plant with the crown 1–2 cm above soil level; a buried crown rots.
Remove spent flowers to keep the plant tidy.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

container.note: 50 cm across, 1 plant per container (RHS).

spacing.note: 60 cm (RHS).

careNotes.text: Put a stake in at planting time (except dwarf types); driving one in later can damage the roots.
Remove spent flowers to encourage more buds.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

spacing.note: 20 cm in rows 45 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Water well before planting the bulbs, then hold off watering until they sprout.
When the leaves start to yellow at the end of the season, cut back on watering.

spacing.note: 30 cm in rows 60 cm apart (TNAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Pinch off fading flowers to encourage new ones.
It likes humidity; mist the leaves regularly if growing it indoors.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

Use an acidic potting mix; in alkaline soil the new leaves turn yellow (chlorosis).

careNotes.text: Let a fresh cutting dry and callus for about 10 days before potting it in a well-drained mix.

spacing.note: 61–91.4 cm (UF/IFAS).

The sap from cut leaves or stems can irritate skin and eyes and stains fabric; wash your hands after handling.

spacing.note: 30 cm in rows 30 cm apart (PAU, field crop).

If the soil dries out and the fronds shed, cut all fronds back to about 5 cm and the plant will regrow.

container.note: 30 cm across, 1 plant per container (KAU).

spacing.note: 45–60 cm (KAU, field crop).

careNotes.text: Keep it humid: stand an indoor anthurium on a tray of moist gravel.
Overwatering causes root rot; yellowing leaves can mean too much water or poor drainage.
It needs little water; overwatering leads to root rot, so let the top of the mix dry first.
Keep it out of draughts and very dry air, which turn the leaves brown.

careNotes.text: Remove spent flowers to encourage more blooms.
To rebloom it needs about six weeks of long nights (14 hours of darkness); keep it away from lights at night.

It climbs if given support, such as a moss- or bark-covered pole, or trails from a hanging basket.

Check regularly for mites, mealybugs and scale, especially on plants kept indoors.

container.note: Figures for potted citrus in general (the lemon named is Meyer lemon): at least 56.8 L of mix, 40.6 cm deep, 43.2 cm across, 1 plant per container (UC ANR).

careNotes.text: Potted citrus dries out fast: in hot weather it may need water every day. Check the soil 15-20 cm down by squeezing a handful; water only when it crumbles.
Don't overwater in the cool season, and never leave the pot standing in water; this rots the roots.

petSafety.note: ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

careNotes.text: Rub off shoots that sprout from the rootstock below the graft, and remove water shoots and crossing branches.
A single tree may fruit poorly: some varieties need pollen from another sapota variety.
On a young grafted mango, pinch off flower clusters as they appear for the first three years so the plant builds its frame first.
Mango responds well to pruning: prune selectively every year, cutting out strong upright shoots and encouraging sideways growth, to keep the tree small.
Plant two different amla varieties together for a good crop.
In March-April, prune and thin out crowded branches to open up more fruiting wood.
Don't let the soil dry out while it flowers: dry plants may drop their blossoms. A mulch helps hold moisture.

Train the vine onto a trellis or pandal.

careNotes.text: For the first two years after planting, remove all the flowers so the vine can establish. In year three, let only about three bunches develop.
A vine in a container needs regular watering through the growing season.

container.note: At least 11.4 L of mix (26.5 L recommended), 1 plant per container (UF/IFAS).

careNotes.text: When the plant flowers and fruits, tie the fruit stalk to a stake so it doesn't topple.
